li.a: Polizia di Stato: Camorra, arrested the fugitive Salvatore Russo
Cooperativa.cl: Italian police captured an important Camorra boss in Naples
Irpinia Oggi: The Irpinian who hid the boss Russo
El País: The Russo clan goes down in history
Corriere della Sera: The Russos like kings, a country at their feet
Stylo24: The Russo clan's push into San Giuseppe Vesuviano

content.p: Pasquale Russo was arrested in the early hours of 1 November 2009 at a farmhouse in Sperone, in Campania. He had spent years on the run. Police had taken his younger brother Salvatore the day before, and within about two days the Carabinieri and the police had also taken Carmine, the youngest of the three. The Napoli anti-mafia prosecutors said the arrests had cut the leadership off from one of the most important clans in the Camorra, the criminal organisation of Campania.

The Russo clan controlled illegal business in Nola, a town on the slopes of the Vesuvio, and in the wider Agro nolano, which Corriere della Sera called the family's fiefdom. El País described the brothers as the ruthless heads of an organisation that ran a protection racket, known as the pizzo, and carried on business ventures in the local economy, in step with the local political world. The family's home village was San Paolo Bel Sito, a commune of about three thousand people that had been dissolved twice because of Camorra infiltration, El País reported.

The Polizia di Stato said that Salvatore and Pasquale led the "nuova famiglia", a faction of the Camorra that was in conflict with Raffaele Cutolo's "nuova camorra" in the nineties. Corriere della Sera called Pasquale the elder brother and the clan's chief, and reported that he had claimed a long friendship with Michele Zaza, a boss from Procida whom it described as the first Camorra member affiliated with Cosa Nostra. Irpinia Oggi wrote that Pasquale had taken over the position once held by Carmine Alfieri, who was arrested by the Carabinieri at Saviano on 11 September 1992. El País gave the same date for Alfieri's arrest.

Salvatore Russo was arrested on Saturday 31 October 2009 at a country house in Somma Vesuviana, a town close to Nola. According to the Polizia di Stato, Squadra mobile officers of Napoli searched the house after they noticed that a wall might hide a space. Behind it they found a hatch leading to a tunnel. Salvatore tried to escape into the tunnel but was caught. He was armed, but the police said he had no chance to resist. The Polizia di Stato named the owner of the house, Luigi Perna, as one of those arrested; El País reported that Perna was held on a charge of complicity.

Pasquale was taken at Sperone, where Irpinia Oggi reported that the Carabinieri had kept the farmhouse under observation for several days, using surveillance and tracking. The officers entered the building in the early hours of the morning, when they believed one of the two fugitives was inside. The farmhouse belonged to Antonio De Sapio, a 53-year-old baker with no criminal record, who was charged with helping a fugitive. Irpinia Oggi reported that Carmine was living in the adjoining house and that the police had a custody order against him for mafia association.

El País described a symbolic detail. Pasquale handed his cane and his coppola, the flat cap that some Camorra bosses treated as a sign of command, to the Carabinieri commander Fabio Cagnazzo. El País compared this with Carmine Alfieri's arrest in 1992.

The accounts differ on timing. El País said the three brothers had been caught within 24 hours, while Corriere della Sera wrote that the Carabinieri and police had closed the matter in two days. El País said the Pasquale arrest happened that morning, while Irpinia Oggi put it at two in the morning.

Pasquale Russo had been sentenced to life imprisonment before his arrest, according to three reports from that week. El País said he had been sentenced to life for several murders and for mafia association. Irpinia Oggi described him as already sentenced to life several times for several killings, mafia association and other offences. Cooperativa.cl reported a life sentence for mafia association and several homicides.

Salvatore's record was reported in similar terms. The Polizia di Stato said he had been sentenced to life for murder and mafia association, and that he had been sought since 1995. El País listed the charges against him as the illegal use of weapons, mafia association, homicide and concealing a body, although El País presented these as the charges against him rather than as verdicts.

Irpinia Oggi wrote that numerous findings from court proceedings had already shown his ties to the leaders of Cosa Nostra, for whom he was said to be the contact in Campania. The paper gave no court or date for these findings.

Napoli prosecutor Giovandomenico Lepore, speaking to the Napoli newspaper Il Mattino as El País reported, said the captures came from investigations that used modern technology and cost a great deal. He complained of cuts to the police budget and warned that a planned law limiting telephone wiretaps would make it impossible to control the territory, in a context of omertà, the local code of silence, and a lack of witnesses willing to testify.

El País dated an operation directed by prosecutor Simona Di Monte to February 2008, when assets worth about €300 million were seized. El País listed buildings, supermarkets, luxury cars and a company producing hazelnuts, which it said was considered the gold of the region. Corriere della Sera said the seizure order described the family as the undisputed masters of the local economy.

Corriere della Sera described the business method in some detail. The family used a company called Russo costruzioni srl, which had no employees, vehicles or capital of its own. Corriere reported that land the family bought suddenly became buildable, without any request. Other firms then built on it and gave the Russo company a share of the apartments for sale. Prosecutors estimated the empire at about a billion euros.

Corriere quoted the seizure order as saying that thousands of citizens had lent their cars to relatives who visited the brothers, and then collected them after they were left in central Nola with the keys inside.

Corriere also reported that the magistrates had written of political cover at every level. They had first investigated a Pdl deputy named Paolo Russo for helping a mafia association from outside it. Corriere described him as a namesake, and that position had been archived.

A 2018 report by Stylo24 said Pasquale and Salvatore had been in prison for almost ten years, and that the clan was still one of the longest-lasting groups in the Nolano area. Citing investigative sources, the paper said a newer generation of the family appeared to be planning to extend its activity into San Giuseppe Vesuviano, where the rival Fabbrocino group was reportedly going through a split. Stylo24 also reported an alleged alliance with the Mazzarella family of Napoli. These were the claims of investigative sources, as Stylo24 reported them, and they were not presented as proven.

The arrests of 2009 ended the fugitive years of two brothers who had run a clan built on extortion, property and political contacts while hiding in farmhouses. The reports agree on the arrests, the life sentences and the seizure of about €300 million. They differ on dates and numbers, and each figure above is credited to the report that gave it.
